note: You are reading the WORLD of a game — the set of places the player moves through and acts in. A place is one location the player occupies (a room, a town, a walkable map area, a building interior). Each place holds interactables — points the player can act on with a verb: examine (look at a thing), take (pick up an item), talk (start a conversation), use (apply an item/condition), move (travel to another place), win (reach the goal). Walkable places also declare a layout: named features (a building, fountain, gate, market stall, clearing...) placed in a rough compass region (northwest, center, south...), with exits at the edges and connections between them. Judge only what is on the page — the places, their kinds, their layout, and the interactables with their verbs and text. You have no knowledge of the author's intent beyond what the world shows. Score on the story's own register: a small, quiet world can reach the top on its own terms; a place is never better for being grand or dense. Mechanical wiring (every place reachable, exits connected, no dead ends) is guaranteed by the build, so it earns a middle level, never the top — the top levels are about places that feel like real, distinct, purposeful locations. For each criterion pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches the world, and cite specific places, features, or interactable text as evidence.

criteria.name: place_distinctness
criteria._authoring: The load-bearing criterion: is each place a DIFFERENT place with its own reason to exist, or are they reskins of one template? Anchor level 0 to the observed failure — interchangeable rooms that differ only by a name/theme string, or a place described so vaguely ('a room with some things') that it has no identity. GATE at threshold 2: a world of interchangeable empty rooms caps the overall at its own score no matter how sensible the wiring or how clean the prose — a reskinned map is a reskinned map.
criteria.description: Is each place a distinct location with its own reason to be in the game — a different function, a different set of things to do — rather than a reskin of the others? Does every place justify its existence?

levels.0: Interchangeable or empty. Places differ only by a name or theme label; they hold the same kinds of interactables doing the same job, or are described so vaguely ('a room with some things') that they have no identity. Swap two place names and nothing would change.
levels.1: Barely differentiated. A couple of places have a hint of their own character, but most are near-duplicates — same interaction pattern, same purpose, restated with different words.
levels.2: Distinct on the surface. Places look different and name different things, but several exist for no clear reason — they add a room to pass through without giving the player a reason to be there.
levels.3: Each place earns its spot. Every place has a clear, different function in the world — this is where you fight, this is where you trade, this is where the secret is — and no two feel like the same place twice.
levels.4: A real, varied world. Every place is unmistakably its own location with a specific role, and together they form a world with texture and progression — moving between them feels like moving through a place that exists, not a menu of rooms.

criteria.name: interaction_purpose
criteria._authoring: Do hotspots earn their place, or are they filler to hit an interactable count? Anchor level 0 to decorative examine hotspots whose text reveals nothing and that gate/reward nothing — present only to fill the space.
criteria.description: Does each interactable earn its place — does it gate something (an item, a route, a flag, a fight), reveal something worth knowing, or reward the player's attention — rather than sit there as decorative filler?

levels.0: Filler. Interactables exist to fill the place; examines reveal nothing, takes hand over items that lead nowhere, and removing most of them would change nothing about playing the world.
levels.1: Mostly inert. A few interactables do real work, but the world is padded with clickable things that neither reward attention nor connect to anything else.
levels.2: Functional. Most interactables do a job — a move, a take, a fight — but they are flat: you act on them because they are there, not because the world made you want to.
levels.3: Purposeful. Nearly every interactable pays off — it opens a route, hands over something you will need, reveals a specific fact, or advances the situation — and the player has a reason to reach for it.
levels.4: Every action rewards. Interactables reward curiosity as well as progress — an examine that tells you something you are glad to know, a take that matters later, a use that clicks into place — and the world would be poorer with any of them cut.

criteria.name: layout_coherence
criteria._authoring: Does the arrangement make spatial sense? Mechanical connectivity (reachable, exits wired, round-trip) is build-guaranteed, so a merely-connected map lands at level 2 — the top levels require the layout to read as a believable arrangement of a real place.
criteria.description: Do the places and their features fit together as a coherent space — features placed sensibly within a place, exits and connections that make spatial sense, a map you could picture standing in?

levels.0: Incoherent. Features and exits are scattered without spatial logic — things sit where they make no sense, or a place's parts do not cohere into any location you could picture.
levels.1: Confused. The space roughly holds together but has jarring placements — a feature in the wrong kind of place, connections that would not make sense if you walked them.
levels.2: Connected and playable. Everything links up and you can get everywhere, but the arrangement is arbitrary — the parts are placed to be reachable, not because that is where they would be.
levels.3: Sensible. Features sit where they belong, exits face the right way, and the connections trace a path you could walk — the layout reads as a plan of a real location.
levels.4: Believable geography. The whole world is spatially convincing — each place is laid out the way that kind of place would be, and the places connect into a map with a clear, natural sense of where things are relative to each other.

criteria.name: observation_texture
criteria._authoring: The examine/use text quality axis, sharing the scenes rubric's fact-not-feeling bar. Anchor level 0 to the observed attractor: mood words in place of physical detail ('eerie room', 'the air feels heavy') and generic labels that name a category, not a specific thing.
criteria.description: Does the text on interactables (examine, take, use) state concrete, specific, physical facts about the thing — its material, condition, what it is for — rather than mood words or vague generic labels?

levels.0: Vague or moody. Text names feelings, not things ('an eerie corner', 'the air feels heavy'), or labels a generic category ('a table', 'some crates') with no specific detail. Nothing is actually observed.
levels.1: Thin. Occasional concrete detail, but most text is generic or reaches for atmosphere instead of naming what is there.
levels.2: Plainly factual. Text states what things are without lapsing into mood, but stays surface-level — accurate and dull, rarely a detail that makes the thing specific.
levels.3: Specific. Text names concrete physical facts — material, condition, use — that make each thing particular to this place, with mood carried by the facts rather than stated.
levels.4: Sharp and grounded. Every observation lands a specific, telling detail that makes the object real and the place vivid, without ever naming a feeling — you can see exactly what the player is looking at.

criteria.name: story_grounding
criteria._authoring: Does the world follow from the premise, or is it a generic adventure map bolted onto any story? Anchor level 0 to interchangeable-fantasy locations (a tavern, a forest, a dungeon) that could belong to any game and owe nothing to this one's premise.
criteria.description: Do the places follow from the game's premise — is this the world THIS story needs, with locations that exist because of what the game is about — rather than a generic set of locations that could belong to any game?

levels.0: Off-the-shelf. The places are generic locations (a tavern, a forest, a dungeon) that owe nothing to this game's premise — lift them into any other game and nothing is lost.
levels.1: Loosely themed. The world wears the premise's costume — the right nouns and colours — but the places themselves are still stock, connected to the story only by their labels.
levels.2: On-theme. The places belong to the premise's genre and setting, but any one of them could be swapped for a similar generic version without the story noticing.
levels.3: Grounded. The places follow from what this game is about — they exist because the premise calls for them, and you could infer the story from the map.
levels.4: Inseparable from the story. The world could belong to no other game — each place is here because of a specific thing this story needs, and the set of places tells you what the game is and where it is going.
